title: Kanban or Scrum? Start With How Work Reaches Your Team
summary: Kanban and Scrum answer different questions. Pick by looking at how work arrives, how much is in progress and what kind of promise your stakeholders need.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
9:20 on a Tuesday. Three support bugs landed before anyone finished their coffee. One product story is waiting on a design answer, two pull requests are stuck in review, and someone asks in the team chat, half joking: "Are we still doing Scrum, or did we turn into Kanban and nobody told us?"

Fair question. Most teams answer it by putting the two frameworks side by side on paper. Scrum has Sprints, a Sprint Goal and five events. Kanban has a board, WIP limits and flow metrics. One looks structured, the other looks flexible. A better starting point is the shape of the work you actually get: how it arrives, how much of it is open at once, and what kind of promise the people around you need from the team.

What each one actually asks of you

Both have short official guides, and they're worth ten minutes before any debate. The Scrum Guide describes Sprints as fixed-length events of one month or less. During a Sprint, "no changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal", though scope "may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned." If the goal stops making sense, the Sprint can be cancelled. The guide is strict about itself too: you can adopt only parts of Scrum, but then "the result is not Scrum."

The Kanban Guide is even shorter. It defines Kanban as "a strategy for optimizing the flow of value through a process" and asks for three practices: define and visualize the workflow, actively manage the items in it, and keep improving it. The people running the system must explicitly control how many items sit between started and finished. That's your WIP limit. Kanban doesn't ask you to drop Sprints, roles or planning, and the guide says it can and should be used to augment other delivery approaches.

So the two don't compete head to head. Scrum is a framework for a team working toward a goal in short cycles. Kanban is a way to manage flow, and it can run inside Scrum or on its own. If the Scrum vocabulary itself feels fuzzy, How Scrum Really Runs walks through it card by card.

Start with how work reaches you

Scrum fits best when most of your work can be shaped a week or two ahead. The team looks at the backlog, picks a batch that serves one goal, and protects enough focus to finish it. That rhythm helps when product direction needs regular conversation, when stakeholders want a predictable review, and when the team benefits from stopping every few weeks to change how it works.

Kanban fits best when work arrives all the time and interruptions are normal: support, operations, platform maintenance, incident follow-ups, small requests from many directions. A perfect Sprint Backlog doesn't help much there. What helps is limiting how much is open, making blocked items obvious, and getting each request from "asked" to "done" without it piling up somewhere in the middle.

Either way, intake needs rules. In Scrum, the team gathers new work, refines it and pulls it into a Sprint. Some still arrives mid-Sprint, and too much of it makes the Sprint Goal meaningless. In Kanban, work can come in continuously, and you still need a policy: who can add work, how urgent items jump the line, how many urgent items can be open at once. A Kanban board without an intake policy becomes a public to-do list where whoever shouts loudest goes first. Flexible doesn't mean rule-free. It means a different set of rules.

Too much WIP is usually the real problem

Many teams think they have a delivery problem when they really have a starting problem. Five developers each holding three tickets makes for a busy-looking board where nothing reaches done. Little's Law shows why. In 1961 John Little proved that, as long-run averages, the number of items in a system equals the rate they arrive times the average time each one spends inside (L = λW). On a board that's roughly stable, that becomes: average cycle time ≈ average WIP ÷ average throughput. If the team finishes about 10 items a week and keeps 30 open, each item takes around three weeks on average. Cut WIP to 15 at the same throughput and it drops to about a week and a half.

That's why Kanban teams limit columns like In Progress, Review and QA. Scrum teams can borrow the habit inside a Sprint. A Sprint Backlog is a plan for the whole Sprint, and nobody said every item has to start on Monday.

Two kinds of predictability

Scrum makes things predictable through cadence. Every Sprint, the team plans, builds, reviews and adjusts. Stakeholders know when the next conversation happens, and the team can forecast from what past Sprints delivered.

Kanban makes things predictable through flow data. The guide names four measures: WIP, throughput, work item age (how long a started item has been open) and cycle time (how long finished items took from start to finish). It also suggests a service level expectation, a forecast such as "85% of work items will be finished in eight days or less." Stakeholders can plan around that, and it comes from your own history instead of a gut feeling.

Scrum asks what the team can likely finish this Sprint. Kanban asks how work moves through the system over time. Neither question is more grown-up than the other. A product team building something new may need the shared focus of a Sprint Goal. A support-heavy team may need the honesty of cycle time and aging items. A services team with client deadlines may want Sprint planning for the commitment and WIP limits inside the Sprint so review and QA don't clog. A young startup may begin with Kanban while priorities change daily, then add a planning rhythm once its direction settles.

Don't pick by vibe

Some teams want Scrum because it feels official. Others want Kanban because it feels lighter. Both instincts can hide the real problem. Scrum won't fix unclear priorities if the Product Owner never has time for the team. Kanban won't fix chaos if every stakeholder can drop work on the board whenever they like. A framework shows you where the pressure is. The calls about ownership, priority and what the team may say no to are still yours to make.

Here's a practical test. Look at the last month of work and answer honestly, without defending the current process:

  • Did most work arrive before the Sprint started, or during it?
  • When you missed, was it bad planning, or too much entering the system at once?
  • Do stakeholders need a fixed review rhythm, or mostly faster movement on small requests?
  • Is the team short on commitment, or carrying too much WIP?

The answers usually point more clearly than any debate about names.

Mixing them on purpose

Plenty of healthy teams end up with a blend: a Sprint Goal for product work, WIP limits on the board, some capacity held back for interrupts, regular retros, and cycle time on the wall so review and QA don't become hidden waiting rooms. People call it Scrumban. The label matters less than knowing which part does which job. The Sprint cadence gives the team a moment to plan and look back. WIP limits keep work moving on the days in between.

Next time the board feels messy, skip "are we doing Scrum or Kanban right?" and ask four things instead: where is work waiting, who controls intake, how much is in progress, and what promise are we trying to make? And if your team calls itself agile and still feels stuck, the framework's name is rarely the issue. Agile Is Dead, Long Live Agile digs into that side.

Try this week

  • Tag last month's tickets as "planned" or "arrived mid-Sprint" and count each pile.
  • Divide the number of items in progress today by last month's weekly throughput. That's your rough average cycle time.
  • Put a WIP limit on your most crowded column, a little below what's in it now.
  • Write down who can add urgent work and how many urgent items may be open at once.
  • Pick the oldest open item on the board and ask what it needs to finish.

faqs.q: What is the main difference between Kanban and Scrum?
faqs.a: Scrum is a framework where a team works toward a Sprint Goal in fixed cycles of one month or less, with set events and accountabilities. Kanban is a strategy for managing flow: visualize the workflow, explicitly limit work in progress, and improve the system using measures like cycle time and throughput. Scrum gives predictability through cadence, Kanban through flow data.

faqs.q: Can a team use Kanban and Scrum together?
faqs.a: Yes. The Kanban Guide says Kanban can and should be used to augment other delivery approaches. A common blend keeps the Sprint Goal and Scrum events, adds WIP limits on the board, holds some capacity for interrupts, and tracks cycle time so review and QA don't become hidden queues.

faqs.q: When is Kanban a better fit than Scrum?
faqs.a: When work arrives continuously and interruptions are normal, as in support, operations, platform maintenance or incident follow-up. If most of your work can't be planned a week or two ahead and the main pain is waiting and overload, flow management with WIP limits usually helps more than Sprint commitments.

faqs.q: How do WIP limits help a team deliver faster?
faqs.a: Little's Law links the three numbers: on a fairly stable board, average cycle time is roughly average WIP divided by average throughput. A team that finishes about 10 items a week while keeping 30 open waits around three weeks per item; with 15 open at the same throughput, it's about a week and a half.
